common_name: IndigoCrisp Blueberry (Crisp-Textured Sweet University of Florida Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark; IndigoCrisp is a low-chill University of Florida release well suited to Gulf Coast zone 8b-9a winters.

directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat and mulched heavily to keep the shallow root system cool and moist. IndigoCrisp was bred by the University of Florida specifically for a distinctively crisp, firm bite that sets it apart from the soft flesh typical of most southern highbush blueberries, along with large berry size and a sweet, well-balanced flavor that holds up well after harvest. It ripens mid-season and carries a low chill requirement, making it a strong performer along the Gulf Coast where many older highbush cultivars underperform. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous new wood.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Blueberry Breeding Program

common_name: Florida Brilliance Strawberry (Early High-Yield UF/IFAS Winter Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in October in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Florida Brilliance is a University of Florida IFAS release bred at the Gulf Coast Research and Education Center as an earlier, redder-fleshed replacement for older commercial short-day strawberries.

directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun. Florida Brilliance was bred at the University of Florida's Gulf Coast Research and Education Center to ripen earlier in the season than the older Florida Radiance and Festival releases it has largely replaced in commercial Gulf-latitude production, with conical fruit that is a deep, glossy red both inside and out and holds excellent flavor even in the warm early-season conditions typical of Gulf Coast fall plantings. As with other short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat it as a winter annual, setting out fresh crowns each fall for harvest from winter through spring rather than expecting the planting to persist as a true perennial. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce fruit rot in humid conditions.
sources: University of Florida IFAS — Gulf Coast Research and Education Center

planting.note: Plant container-grown or rooted cutting transplants in spring; Florea begins bearing at a young age and ripens its main crop earlier than most Gulf South fig cultivars, giving a useful head start before the peak-summer rainy season that causes fruit souring in later-ripening figs.

directions: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Florea is prized for ripening its light amber-brown, honey-flavored fruit notably earlier in the season than most named fig cultivars, often starting well before the peak summer humidity that brings on souring and splitting in later-ripening types. It is self-fertile like all common figs, needs no pollinator, and tends toward a smaller, more compact tree than vigorous types like Celeste or Brown Turkey, making it a reasonable choice for a large container or a tight garden spot. Fruit quality is best picked fully ripe and soft, since it can taste bland if harvested early. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and control size; heavy pruning sacrifices the following season's breba crop.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Fig Production in Louisiana

common_name: Osborn Prolific Fig (Heavy-Bearing Purple-Brown Heirloom Fig)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or rooted cutting transplants in spring; Osborn Prolific is an old English heirloom fig valued for heavy, reliable fruiting and good cold hardiness for a fig, tolerating winter dieback and regrowing to bear the same season.

directions: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Osborn Prolific is a long-grown English heirloom fig noted for exceptionally heavy, consistent crops of medium purple-brown fruit with sweet, strawberry-pink flesh and good flavor even in cooler summers. It is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, and its relatively strong cold hardiness for a fig — regrowing reliably from the roots or lower trunk after a hard winter — makes it a forgiving choice at the cooler edge of fig-growing range as well as in the milder Gulf South. Fruit ripens over a long midsummer-to-fall window rather than all at once, which spreads out the harvest for home use. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and shape the tree; heavy pruning reduces the following season's breba crop.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Fig Fact Sheet
